question: Net Profit from the Income Statement flows into which line on the Balance Sheet?
before: Net profit added to Retained Earnings in Equity on BS. Cash affected through CFS not directly from profit. Receivables affected by revenue. Borrowings unrelated to profit.
after:
Concept: Net Profit represents the bottom line of the Income Statement—the earnings available to shareholders after all expenses, taxes, and interest are deducted. This profit does not stay as cash on the Balance Sheet; instead, it flows into the equity section, specifically Retained Earnings (also called Reserves & Surplus in Indian financial statements), where it accumulates year after year unless distributed as dividends.

Why this is correct: The Income Statement and Balance Sheet are linked through the profit flow. Net Profit increases the equity of the company. In the Balance Sheet, retained earnings represent cumulative profits earned by the company that have not been paid out to shareholders as dividends. Each period's Net Profit (minus any dividends) is added to the opening Retained Earnings balance to arrive at the closing Retained Earnings.

Why the others are wrong: A) Cash & Cash Equivalents—Net Profit does not directly become cash. Profit is an accounting concept; the actual movement of cash is tracked in the Cash Flow Statement. A company can be highly profitable yet have low cash if it collects receivables slowly or invests heavily in inventory. B) Trade Receivables—These arise from revenue recognition under accrual accounting, not from net profit. Revenue is the top line of the Income Statement; receivables represent the unpaid portion of that revenue, unrelated to the bottom-line profit figure. D) Long-Term Borrowings—These are liabilities raised through debt financing and have no direct link to profit generation. Borrowings are determined by financing decisions, not by operational performance.

Intuition: Understanding this link is fundamental to equity research. When you see high net profit but flat retained earnings, it signals large dividend payouts or potential one-time gains. When you see retained earnings growing much slower than cumulative profits, it hints at cash distributions or write-downs. This flow validates that the three statements—Income, Balance Sheet, and Cash Flow—must reconcile logically.
